summary.core_message: The variety and performance of possible displays and processors create different requirements for visual UI design and may limit available design options.
summary.design_implication: Before designing, teams must understand the screen's hardware capabilities and limitations and consider the display together with input and output devices.

criteria.name: Size
criteria.design_relevance: Product UI displays may be significantly smaller than other digital touchpoints, affecting layout, typography, interaction, and information density.

criteria.name: Resolution
criteria.design_relevance: Resolution determines how much detail, typography, icons, and UI components can be shown clearly.

criteria.name: Color representation
criteria.design_relevance: Color capability determines whether full BDDS color schemes, brand assets, semantic status colors, and contrast patterns can be used directly or need adaptation.

pre_design_checks: Evaluate the hardware capabilities and limits before visual design starts.
Treat the display and input/output devices as one unit.
Determine minimum display requirements based on font size and input/output needs.
Determine maximum display requirements based on budget, technical feasibility, and project parameters.
technology_trends: Displays are getting larger and higher resolution with expanded colors.
Classical display shapes are being dissolved, for example through curved displays.
Displays may be replaced or extended by 3D or holographic output.
Haptic input methods are being extended by touchless gestures.
Visual output methods can be extended by haptic feedback, for example vibration.

categories.name: Simple displays
categories.definition: Displays with fixed or limited visual structures, constrained color representation, and reduced visual design flexibility compared with high-resolution color displays.
categories.context: Technological advances are shrinking the differences between simple displays and other digital touchpoints. Some design concepts from wearables, smartwatches, and smartphones may already be transferable to simple product UI displays.
constraints: Typography may be replaced by LEDs, Bosch pixel font, or Bosch 7-segment font
Touch interaction may not be available
Physical controls or keyboard input may be required
Possible loss of design language due to technical restrictions

subtypes.name: Segment displays
characteristics: Fixed structure
Limited color representation
Segment clusters can be turned on and off
Predefined symbols and text appear in fixed locations
Uses segment fonts, for example 7, 14, or 16 segments
Inverted or dark display can offer better contrast and a more modern appearance
No backlighting or only single-color backlighting across the entire display area
Battery-operated products may avoid or temporarily use backlighting to save energy
implications: Design must work within predefined symbol and text positions.
Text and icons cannot be freely composed like on full graphical displays.
Contrast and legibility are central because visual differentiation options are limited.

subtypes.name: Dot-matrix displays
characteristics: Individually designable compared with fixed segment displays
Still limited in color selection
implications: Allows more flexible pixel-based layouts than segment displays.
Design must remain robust under constrained color and resolution conditions.

subtypes.name: Monochrome TFT displays
characteristics: Individually designable
Limited color selection
Requires high contrast for good readability in all conditions
implications: Prioritize contrast, hierarchy, and clear shapes over color-based meaning.
Avoid relying on BDDS color schemes without monochrome adaptation.

subtypes.name: Analogue displays
characteristics: Can be understood as the simplest form of a display because they communicate information
Can communicate by backlighting a symbol
Can communicate by color, for example status or warning colors
implications: Information must be encoded through simple signals such as light, color, or activation state.
Semantic clarity is essential because there may be no text or detailed graphics.

brand_elements.general_rule: Brand elements must be used, but may need alternatives when they cannot be displayed in their original form because of color, size, or screen limitations.
allowed_or_recommended: Activity Indicator in a monochrome variant
Symbol/logotype in black or white when no physical logo is present
not_allowed_or_discouraged: Displaying the Supergraphic as plain black and white
Using the Supergraphic under a header on plain black-and-white displays
brand_elements.reasoning: The Supergraphic depends on brand-specific color behavior and cannot be meaningfully reduced to black-and-white or grayscale without losing intended brand expression.

color.rule: All colors are reduced to black and white on monochrome displays.
exceptions: Cases where white is the dominant color
Cases where white is the interaction color
color.design_note: Some BDDS color schemes and components cannot be used without adaptation on monochrome displays.

categories.name: Complex displays
categories.definition: Higher-capability displays, such as TFT LCD displays and LCD touchscreens, that can represent color and support richer UI patterns.
categories.context: The larger the display, the more its operating paradigms resemble other digital touchpoints, especially software and mobile apps.

subtypes.name: TFT LCD displays and LCD touchscreens
characteristics: Can display color
Can support richer visual and interaction patterns
Viewing angle and lighting conditions affect visual quality
High contrast is important for readability
On LED displays, each segment can display all possible colors
implications: Use BDDS core components where possible.
Use Bosch Icons and Bosch Sans Regular and Bold.
Use BDDS color schemes with attention to contrast and context of use.
Consider environmental visibility, viewing angles, lighting, and device context.

brand_elements.general_rule: All graphic elements can be displayed in good quality on high-resolution color displays.
brand_elements.supergraphic_rule: Use of the Supergraphic is mandatory on high-resolution color displays.
brand_elements.note: Several implementation options are available for brand elements and should be selected according to the brand elements guidance.

mandatory_or_core: Use Bosch Sans in Regular and Bold
Use the Supergraphic on high-resolution color displays
optional_or_contextual: Additional lighting elements, for example LED ring for Supergraphic

then: Reduce color logic to black/white representation.
Do not use the Supergraphic in grayscale or plain black-and-white.
Use monochrome alternatives for brand elements when needed.
Use predefined symbols and text positions.
Avoid design patterns requiring flexible layout or typography.
Use BDDS core components and color schemes.
Use Bosch Icons and Bosch Sans.
Use brand elements in good quality.
Include the Supergraphic as mandatory brand expression.
Design interaction around physical controls, keyboard, or other input devices.
Consider display and input/output hardware as one combined interface system.

recommended_for: Choosing between simple and complex display design rules
Prompting AI agents to evaluate display limitations before UI generation
Creating rule-based checks for Product UI brand compliance
Mapping hardware constraints to UI design constraints
not_a_substitute_for: Formal approval from Bosch brand/design governance
Accessibility and readability testing under real operating conditions
